title: Sleep strengthens successor representations of learned sequences in humans
experiments_summary: Thirty healthy adults participated in an experiment combining behavioral tasks, high-density EEG (including polysomnography), and deep neural network (DNN)-based representational similarity analysis (RSA). The protocol involved: (1) a pre-learning perceptual task in which participants viewed 50 images from five categories (objects, faces, scenes, letter strings, body parts) and performed a 1-back repetition detection task; (2) a 'Memory Arena' learning task in which the same 50 images were organized into fixed temporal sequences and spatial locations, with participants learning to criterion (≥66% pairwise sequence accuracy) through alternating exposure and test blocks; (3) a pre-sleep memory test; (4) a ~2-hour nap with concurrent polysomnographic EEG recording; (5) an interference task re-encoding the same images in a different sequence order; (6) a post-sleep memory test; and (7) a post-learning repetition of the perceptual task. EEG was recorded throughout wake tasks (64-channel system, 500 Hz, re-referenced to common average, preprocessed with downsampling, high-pass filtering, ICA artifact removal, and z-scoring). To assess successor and predecessor representations, multivariate linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was performed using cross-session decoding: classifiers were trained on pre-learning perceptual task EEG data for four image categories and tested on post-learning perceptual task data, with predictions compared against the category of neighboring items (predecessor, successor, second predecessor, second successor) in the learned sequence. Decoding accuracies were compared against chance (25%) using cluster-based permutation tests. Correlations between successor decoding accuracy and pre-sleep, post-sleep, and interference memory performance were computed using Spearman correlation. To characterize the representational format of successor information, RSA was applied by constructing time-resolved pairwise EEG similarity matrices (Spearman correlations across channels) and comparing them to representational similarity matrices derived from each of the seven layers of a pretrained AlexNet DNN (conv1–conv5, fc6, fc7). DNN current-image matrices were regressed out from EEG similarity matrices before correlating residuals with DNN successor matrices. A two-way repeated-measures ANOVA (session × DNN layer) with cluster-based permutation testing assessed session-by-layer interactions. A 'representational shift' index was computed by correlating layer-specific EEG–successor similarity changes with layer hierarchy and tested against zero using one-sample t-tests. Sleep data were staged according to AASM guidelines using automated tools (YASA, Somnobot) validated by experienced scorers. SOs were detected by bandpass filtering (0.3–1.25 Hz) and identifying zero-crossing events with amplitude exceeding mean+1 SD. Spindles were detected by bandpass filtering (12–16 Hz), RMS thresholding, and requiring ≥6 oscillatory cycles. SO–spindle coupling was defined as spindle envelope maxima occurring within SO onset-to-offset intervals, and coupling strength was quantified using pairwise phase consistency (PPC) at electrode Cz via Hilbert-transform-derived SO phase. Proportions of each sleep stage and PPC values were correlated (Spearman) with successor representational strength and representational shift indices derived from the identified significant time windows.
